Adopt vLLM 0ac9dcb for standalone GPU serving (#11241)

Use the [published vLLM
release](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261113-0ac9dcb157ee)
at `0ac9dcb157ee` for standalone GPU serving with Torch 2.14.1 and CUDA

RMSNorm rounding, stale FP8 padding scales and missing ShortConv decode
outputs. The GPU launcher installs this stack in its isolated serving
environment. Trainer adoption stays in #11307; TPU adoption stays in

The x86_64 and aarch64 wheels passed the [H100 and GB200 release
gates](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/actions/runs/43379837147).
Fresh Snowball checks passed 64 prompts each at one and two pipeline
stages, with compilation and CUDA graphs enabled. Maximum
token-probability errors were 0.124960 and 0.124768, respectively,
against the unchanged 0.125 bound. Both results are close to the
acceptance bound.

The affected CPU suite has 1,000 passes, nine failures and one
collection skip. The nine failures match the independent main `200c32d`
baseline: missing Python pidfd support, hash fixtures and a NixOS
shell-path assumption. Required lint passes; advisory review has no
findings. Rollback restores `marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac` and
its generated pins.

commits.message:
[sft] Normalize tool calls in the pinned SFT campaign (#11498)

Add a campaign-specific experiment that rewrites supported notebook,
shell and control calls into real harness operations. Notebook cells
share a visible persistent IPython kernel. Historical observations
remain source evidence; the converter does not reexecute source
programs.

The runner accepts only three pinned selection catalogs and one
Llama-3-style tokenizer. Unknown chat formats, tool sets and selection
schemas fail with a pointer to the README's scope limits. Terminus,
dropped sources, ARC and unsupported call structures receive no
converted replacement. Receipt-bound archives preserve provenance and
source-row identities for independently audited overlays.

A 17,793-row pinned canary yielded 3,929 independently audited changes,
11,325 tool-free rows and 2,539 residual rows. The checks validate the
adapter and serialized export, not the correctness of the original
tasks.

[task-curation] Add NuminaMath-LEAN training data for the Lean proof grader (#11095)

Add NuminaMath-LEAN as Lean training data for the #10879 grader. The
branch is stacked on #10879; the commits after it are new.

The source starts from the 9,475 NuminaMath-LEAN rows where people wrote
both the Lean statement and the proof. Each task asks for a proof of the
frozen statement, and the row's own proof is its golden control, kept
out of the prompt.

A row is left out when it comes from MATH's test split, which holds
MATH-500; when Prime's Lean environments list it as broken or
misformalized (their lists, pinned by sha256); when its statement
doesn't compile with our toolchain, uses the old `∑ x in s` syntax, runs
code, or proves other theorems before the target; when its proof uses
`native_decide` or `sorry` or runs code; or when it repeats a miniF2F,
ProofNet-Verified or PutnamBench problem (`eval_overlap.py`).

That leaves 6,834 statements. The human proofs of 4,035 of them compile
without `sorry` on Lean v4.34.1 and Mathlib v4.34.1, exactly as the
golden control submits them, and only those become tasks, so every task
has a golden control that compiles, whether or not the pipeline samples
it. All 4,035 statements validate with the grader's reference check. The
list of passing proofs is `numina_proofs.json`, and `check_statements.py
numina --write-proofs` regenerates it.

Next I can add the 2,654 rows with a human statement and a Kimina-Prover
proof as a separate source, as asked in review :)

Part of #10842

Co-authored-by: Matt Wittmann <matt.wittmann@openathena.ai>

commits.author: Robertboy18
commits.message:
[task-curation] Add a Lean v4.34.1 proof grader and ProofNet-Verified (#10879)

First step for the Lean effort, following Mark's suggestion to start by
getting Lean data into TaskTrove. This adds:

- **A Lean proof grader** (Lean v4.34.1 + Mathlib v4.34.1) that checks
proofs by kernel replay, using Prime Intellect's `lean-export` and
`lean-verify`. A proof scores 1 only if it proves exactly the given
statement using Lean's three standard axioms: `propext`,
`Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. Anything else scores 0, including
`sorry`, `native_decide`, proofs that skip the kernel check and proofs
that crash their own compile.
- **How it runs:** each grade gets a fresh sandbox. The proof's compile
and export run as their own unprivileged user, and the reference compile
and `lean-verify` run as root.
- **ProofNet-Verified as an eval source:** 365 of its 367 rows. Row 35
ships its own proof instead of `sorry`, and row 351 repeats row 168.
- **Tests**, including three real ProofNet rows graded end to end. A
short proof takes about 30 s to grade and fits in 8 GB.

A broken statement, a grader failure or a proof too slow for
`lean-verify` shows up as an infra error; anything else the proof causes
scores 0.

Next I can add training data from NuminaMath-LEAN :)

Part of #10842

commits.author: yonromai
commits.message:
[rl] Recover native continuations from their own checkpoints (#11330)

A continuation run can start from a supplied native checkpoint and
recover its own progress after interruption. Automatic recovery prefers
the current run’s latest checkpoint. It uses the starting checkpoint
only when the run has none. Without either, it starts fresh.

`SkyRLSpec.starting_checkpoint` is an artifact dependency whose identity
and resolved path participate in the run’s fingerprint. It requires
`resume_mode=latest` and no recipe `trainer.resume_path`. Conflicting
resume settings fail validation. The `generate` and
`terminal_bench_generate` recipes reject native starting checkpoints.

The initial import restores native model, optimizer, scheduler and
trainer state, while starting the configured dataset from the beginning.
Optional step and token-counter resets apply only to that import.
Recovery preserves this run’s saved counters and, by default, data
progress. A corrupt marker, missing selected checkpoint or load error
stops the run.

The continuation owns its checkpoint output. Changing its starting
checkpoint requires a new RL artifact version. Before retrying,
interrupted runs compare the requested checkpoint input with the one
recorded in the previous launch. Completed immutable artifact versions
reject configuration changes through the existing fingerprint check.
Training limits remain absolute step targets.

CPU tests compare continued and recovered training with an uninterrupted
run. Model, optimizer and scheduler state must match exactly. The
checkpoint format and native restore backend are unchanged.

---------

Co-authored-by: Romain Yon <1596570+yonromai@users.noreply.github.com>

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[belay] Add the Data Belay for testing new training datasets (#11019)

👨 This PR introduces "Data Belay", a procedure to assess the value of a
dataset. tldr: we take the existing pretraining data sample $$D_{old}$$,
and replace $$p$$ of it with a sample from a new dataset $$D_{new}$$. We
compare perplexity evals (Paloma, Uncheatable, and perplexity on Eval
Policy tasks) against 2 controls:
  * gain vs $$D_{old}$$
     * is $$p$$ of new data better than just more $$D_{old}$$?
* harm vs $$D_{old}$$ with $$p$$ replaced by text "no" eval captures
(e.g. Japanese or Arabic)
* is $$p$$ of new data worse than $$p$$ of "useless" data on any eval?

The side-effect is that all data we add should have some existing eval,
or a new eval needs to be added to justify the new data.

This procedure should work for both:
1. I have a new dataset - is it useful?
2. I have a new way to filter data - is it useful?
In this case the user specifies 2 experiments, a) new data without
filter and b) new data after the filter. If the filter is useful the b)
would win.

<hr>

🤖 Add `experiments/data_belay` and a `data-belay` CLI that run this
procedure on main's fast-track dense model
(`experiments/grug/fast_track/launch.py --dense`, at its baseline
budget), at three rungs (d512, d768, d1024) with 3 seeds each:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check` | pins the dataset revision, classifies its card license, and
estimates its tokens and epochs at each rung |
| `prepare`, `prepare-datakit` | tokenizes a seeded sample of a Hugging
Face dataset, or of Datakit sources' normalized output, into a cache |
| `train` | trains one seed of an arm with the fast-track launcher, on
`cw-us-east-02a` |
| `score` | writes each finished run's choice loss and accuracy, outside
the runs' 30-day TTL |
| `report` | prints the verdict, how much of each arm's data its runs
read, and the ladder's next step; `--against` judges a filtered
candidate against its unfiltered source |

`launch.py` gains `--mix-cache` and `--mix-share` (a second train cache
at a constant share), `--eval-policy-answer-bpb` (Eval Policy
gold-answer BPB as validation steps), `--seed`, `--output-path` and
`--priority`. Without them a run is unchanged. Its model builder is now
public, `h100_ladder_model`, so the scorer builds the model that the
launcher trains.

There are six eval groups: Paloma, Uncheatable, and the Eval Policy
groups knowledge, commonsense, math and code. A group is `better` when
its interval against the control is below 0 and its gain is at least 1%,
and `worse` when its interval against the dilution references is past
its harm limit, max(1%, 2.5 seed SDs of the d512 control). A rung is a
yes (`helps` or `trade-off`) when some group is better and none is
worse. A candidate climbs until two consecutive rungs say no, unless
some group is below 0 at the second. The answer is yes when d768 and
d1024 both say yes, and mixed when they disagree.

The method was validated on the dense model of Belay's `vanilla` Track
(on `marin_belay_v1_recipe`), which reads the same base cache with the
same tokenizer:

| Validation arm, share | d512 | d768 | d1024 | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FineMath-4plus, 5% | helps | trade-off | trade-off | yes |
| FineMath-4plus, 20% | helps | helps | helps | yes |
| FineMath-4plus, 50% | trade-off | hurts | hurts | no |
| OpenWebMath, 20% | helps | helps | helps | yes |
| OpenCoder synthetic code, 20% | trade-off | trade-off | trade-off |
yes |
| OpenCoder web code, 20% | helps | no gain | no gain | no |
| FineWeb-2 Chinese, 20% | no gain | no gain | | no |
| FineWeb, 20% | no gain | helps | helps | yes |
| FineWeb, 50% | hurts | hurts | hurts | no |
| FineWeb-Edu, 20% | trade-off | helps | helps | yes |
| FineWeb-Edu, 50% | hurts | hurts | hurts | no |
| FineWeb-Edu against FineWeb, 50% | hurts | hurts | hurts | no |
| Cosmopedia web samples, 20% | no gain | no gain | no gain | no |
| Null: control seeds 6–8 | no gain | no gain | no gain | no |

The dilution references exist at 20% only, so the 5% and 50% arms were
judged for harm against the control. `report` now refuses that: at a
share without references it takes `--against`, or prints the commands
that build the references at that share. Five arms stopped at d768 under
the first ladder and ran on to d1024 under the current one: all five
stay no, and the null arm stays `no gain`. FineWeb at 50% is `hurts` on
code alone (+7.2%), judged against the control; at 20%, judged against
the references, it is a yes. A sweep of 183 Datakit sources at 20%
(1,431 runs) ended 61 yes, 15 mixed and 107 no. The 1% gain floor
changed one of those answers (Nemotron's wiki rewrite, from mixed to no)
and no validation verdict; before it, 58 of the 106 nos were sources
that no eval measures. There is no contamination scan yet (#11480), so a
gain on a single eval set needs a check for leakage.

On the fast-track model, five validation arms reran at d512 and d768 and
the null arm at d512, each judged on seeds 0–2:

| Arm, share | d512, vanilla | d512, fast-track | d768, vanilla | d768,
fast-track |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FineMath-4plus, 20% | helps | helps | helps | helps |
| FineWeb-Edu, 20% | trade-off | helps | helps | helps |
| FineWeb, 20% | no gain | trade-off | helps | helps |
| Cosmopedia web samples, 20% | no gain | no gain | no gain | no gain |
| FineWeb, 50% | hurts | hurts | hurts | hurts |
| Null: control seeds 6–8 | no gain | no gain | no gain | not run |

Across the 30 pairs of arm and group at each rung, the two models' gains
correlate at 0.99. The one rung that turns from no to yes, FineWeb at
20% at d512, has the gains the vanilla model shows at d768. The
fast-track control's seeds vary less (Paloma SD 0.11% at d512, against
0.38%). Without the 1% floor, its null arm was `helps` at d512 on math
−0.56% [−1.09%, −0.03%]. There are no fast-track controls or dilution
references at d1024 yet: the first candidate to reach d1024 needs 15
runs trained for them.

<details>
<summary>Commands in detail</summary>

`check` allows the licenses on the Blue Oak Council's [list of
permissive licenses](https://blueoakcouncil.org/list) (every rating,
version 16), OpenMDW, and the data licenses CC BY, CC BY-SA and ODC-By,
which the list does not cover. It refuses NC and ND licenses. It sends
any other license to a person, and `prepare` refuses it: that covers
`other`, a missing license, and an extra license that is not allowed. It
also refuses a share that reads the dataset more than 4 times at the
largest rung. `prepare` tokenizes a seeded random sample of whole files
into a cache in `us-east-02a`, capped by documents per tokenize shard.
`prepare-datakit` does the same for one or more Datakit registry
sources. It sizes each file from its Parquet metadata, and records the
sources' card licenses without refusing them, since the registry already
admits the sources.

`train` writes under its own 30-day TTL root,
`tmp/ttl=30d/data_belay/runs/`, apart from Belay's runs. It names a
treatment run from its cache (dataset, config, share, and a hash of the
cache path). It refuses a run id that W&B already has, and a rung that
reads the cache more than 4 times. `score` runs one H100 Iris job per
batch of finished runs, and refuses a run whose executor status is not
SUCCESS. It writes `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/data_belay/choice/<run
id>.json`, so verdicts can be recomputed after the checkpoints expire.
`report` refuses a run that `score` has not written. Under the verdict
it prints the tokens each arm read, the epochs of its cache and the
fraction of the dataset seen, and the ladder line gives the epochs at
each rung. It takes the share and the tokens trained from the runs' W&B
config. The candidate is judged against the dilution references that
trained at its share, and `--against`, which reads both arms at the same
seeds, refuses two arms at different shares. `--share` takes a whole
percent, so the run label (`p20`) names the share exactly.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Metrics</summary>

The Eval Policy groups hold 11 non-agentic benchmarks (#10197). Small
ladder models score near chance on them, so most tasks use gold-answer
BPB, with the loss masked to the answer tokens after the prompt.
MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA (MC1) use choice loss, `−log2
softmax(ll)[gold]`, where `ll` is each option's log-likelihood summed
over its tokens. Answer BPB misses a gain in the gold answer's margin
over the distractors, and choice loss sees it. Knowledge averages its
three tasks relative to the control's mean at the rung, because TriviaQA
stays on answer BPB. Commonsense stays on answer BPB: PIQA's and
WinoGrande's choice loss varied about 4 times as much between control
seeds. GPQA is gated and left out. BoolQ is logged but left out of the
verdict: its answer is one yes/no token, and its BPB varied 10.7%
between control seeds. Paloma is one group of six because #10108 found
that Paloma macro alone misorders data selections.

The control has 6 seeds at d512 and 3 at d768 and d1024. `report`
computes the harm limits from the current d512 control seeds, so they
follow a change of model or base mix, and `noise --rung d512` prints
them. On main's model they are 1% for Paloma, Uncheatable, knowledge and
commonsense, 1.19% for math and 1.88% for code. On the vanilla Track,
seed SD is 0.4–0.5% on Paloma and Uncheatable and up to 1.2% on the Eval
Policy groups, higher than in #10108, because a seed sets both the model
init and the data order, and the limits were 1.0% to 3.0%. Main's limits
change no verdict at d512 or d768.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Why harm is against the dilution references, and the ladder
rules</summary>

The references are four Datakit sources at 20% whose text no eval
measures, in scripts the English evals do not share: ClimbLab Japanese,
and FinePDFs Chinese, Thai and Arabic. Each counts as one value, the
mean of its seeds, because they differ from each other by more than
their seeds do. On main's model, giving up 20% of the base mix costs
every group 1.3% to 3.6% on its own at d512 and d768, past every group's
harm limit. In the Datakit sweep, with harm against the control, 88 of
the 477 rung verdicts were `hurts`, and none of their 131 failing groups
is past its limit against the references. OpenCoder synthetic code was a
no under that judge: its Paloma and Uncheatable costs at d768, +2.4% and
+2.7%, are +0.8% and +0.6% against the references.

One rung is not enough: web code went from `helps` at d512 to `no gain`
at d768. A gain inside its interval at d768 can clear it at d1024. Of 49
sweep sources stopped at d768 that ran on to d1024, 6 were trade-offs
there, each with its gaining group below 0 at d768. Running on costs
runs only, since a yes still needs both top rungs: in 4,000 simulated
null arms, none ended yes at the fast-track model's seed spread and 0.3%
at the vanilla Track's (1.1% at either without the 1% gain floor). A
rule that also let `no gain` at one top rung agree with a yes at the
other raised that to 8.9%, so it was dropped.
</details>

<details>
<summary>Validation details</summary>

| Validation arm, share | Main change at the top rung (negative is
better) |
|---|---|
| FineMath-4plus, 5% | math −8.3%, others within noise |
| FineMath-4plus, 20% | math −16.7%, code −4.0% |
| FineMath-4plus, 50% | math −23.5%; Paloma +2.2%, Uncheatable +3.4% |
| OpenWebMath, 20% | math −8.5%, others within noise |
| OpenCoder synthetic code, 20% | code −5.3%; Paloma +2.2%, Uncheatable
+2.4% |
| OpenCoder web code, 20% | all groups within noise |
| FineWeb-2 Chinese, 20% | every group +2–4% |
| FineWeb, 20% | commonsense −2.3%, Paloma −1.3%; code +2.0% (−0.3%
against the references) |
| FineWeb, 50% | code +7.2%; commonsense −4.8%, knowledge −3.7% |
| FineWeb-Edu, 20% | knowledge −3.5%, commonsense −1.8%, code +0.7% |
| FineWeb-Edu, 50% | code +7.4%; knowledge −6.3%, commonsense −3.4% |
| FineWeb-Edu against FineWeb, 50% | Paloma +2.0%; knowledge −2.7% |
| Cosmopedia web samples, 20% | all groups within ±1.5% |
| Null: control seeds 6–8 | all groups within noise |

Changes are against the control, except FineWeb-Edu against FineWeb. The
README has every rung's group deltas.

The null arm, FineMath at 5% and 50%, Cosmopedia, OpenWebMath and
FineWeb-Edu at 20% tested the method, with expectations written down
before their runs.
- The null arm met its expectation: no group is `better` or `worse` at
any rung.
- FineMath's dose response met it: the math gain and the cost on general
text both grow with the share at every rung.
- Cosmopedia did not: it was expected to improve knowledge or
commonsense, and no task in either group moved.
- OpenWebMath met it: a yes, with about half of FineMath's math gain.
- FineWeb-Edu at 20% met it: a yes, with knowledge and commonsense
`better` at every rung.

These runs were the fresh test of choice loss, whose rule and harm limit
were fixed before them.

`score` also writes multiple-choice accuracy (cloze `acc_norm`). At
d768, the control is above chance on three tasks: SciQ, ARC-Easy and
PIQA. On those, FineWeb-Edu at 50% beats the control by 2.6 points
[+1.8, +3.4], and beats FineWeb by 1.9 points [+0.9, +3.0]. Cosmopedia
is flat, which agrees with its verdict. Answer BPB missed FineWeb-Edu's
gain over FineWeb, and choice loss sees it (knowledge −1.6% at d512 and
−2.2% at d768). Choice loss also penalizes long options, because it sums
log-likelihoods: on MMLU-Pro, the most likely option is right 8.3% of
the time, below the 10% chance rate.
</details>
